title: Bram and the Vow
premise: Vesper Thackeray, a guarded pastry chef on the brink of losing his café, has spent ten years exchanging anonymous letters with a stranger who once answered a note he left in a library book. When Bram Hollis — the letter writer, newly returned from abroad after inheriting his grandmother's crumbling house — moves in next door, neither recognizes the other at first, and an easy friendship deepens into something neither planned. As Vesper's debts come due and Bram's inheritance forces him to choose between selling the house and staying, their identities finally surface, threatening everything they've built. In the end, Vesper must risk the café he saved and the heart he sealed away, choosing Bram over the safe, past-tense life he'd promised himself.
about_author: Lena Eriksen is a former bakery counter girl turned novelist who writes love stories about people who are bad at asking for what they want. She lives in a coastal town where she still judges cafés by their cardamom buns.

chapters.title: Three Missed Payments
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Opening on a brutal morning: a final notice pinned under the café door, a failed croissant batch, and Vesper's ritual of rereading one old letter before locking his feelings away. Establishes his debt, his craft, and his rule against present-tense love. Emotional beat: weary defiance masking loneliness.

chapters.title: The Man Next Door
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram arrives to claim the inherited house beside the café — a place full of his grandmother's things and his own guilt for staying away so long. He wanders into Vesper's café, and their first conversation sparks something unguarded in both of them. Emotional beat: tentative curiosity, two strangers circling something familiar.

chapters.title: Sugar Work
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Bram starts lingering at the café, fixing the wobbly tables, learning to pipe frosting badly while Vesper pretends not to enjoy the company. A developer's offer looms over both properties, quietly raising stakes. Emotional beat: warmth creeping past defenses neither will admit are down.

chapters.title: Letters, Past Tense
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Flashbacks woven through the present reveal the decade of letters — how they began, what they meant, why Vesper stopped answering when real life got too close. He almost tells Bram about them, then doesn't. Emotional beat: nostalgia sharpening into fear that honesty costs too much.

chapters.title: The House That Remembers
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Sorting his grandmother's attic, Bram finds her correspondence — including letters she wrote to a young baker down the street, and a photograph suggesting the pen pal chain runs through this very neighborhood. The bank sets a deadline on the house. Emotional beat: grief entangled with dawning connection.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A storm knocks out power; the two share candlelight, wine, and nearly a confession — until Vesper deflects and Bram, stung, retreats. The developer circles again, offering Vesper a lifeline that would mean demolishing Bram's house. Emotional beat: longing curdling into miscommunication.

chapters.title: What the Contract Says
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Cornered by the bank, Vesper signs a provisional deal with the developer to save the café — the same deal that dooms the house next door. Guilt-ridden, he avoids Bram, and the distance between them hardens. Emotional beat: self-betrayal dressed up as survival.

chapters.title: The Name at the Bottom
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Packing the house in defeat, Bram discovers Vesper's handwriting in the oldest letter — the truth of their decade-long correspondence laid bare. He confronts Vesper publicly, in the café, demanding to know if any of it was real or just another thing Vesper kept safely in the past. Emotional beat: raw betrayal meeting long-overdue exposure.

chapters.title: Everything on the Line
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Climax. With demolition crews scheduled and the café's fate sealed by contract, Vesper chooses at last: he tears up the developer's deal, gambles the café on a desperate community bake sale Bram secretly organized, and confesses everything — the letters, the fear, the love in present tense. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into courage.

chapters.title: Present Tense
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Resolution. The bake sale saves the café; the neighborhood rallies to restore the house instead of selling it. Bram stays, and the two write one final letter together — signed by both names, dated today. Emotional beat: quiet joy, found family, and love finally allowed its future.
